introduction.text: The Arch of Titus is a 1st‑century AD triumphal arch in Rome that commemorates Emperor Titus's victory over the Jewish rebellion and serves as a key monument in Roman architecture and Jewish history.

history.description: The arch was erected in the 1st century AD to honor Titus and the Roman victory over the Jewish rebellion.
Panels on the arch depict the triumphal procession of 71 AD after the Roman victory in Jerusalem.
The arch was constructed around 81 AD by Emperor Domitian to commemorate his brother Titus.
During Pope Paul IV's papacy (1555–1599), the arch became a site for yearly oaths of submission by Jewish elders.
In 1716, Adriaan Reland published a work on the spoils of the temple visible on the Arch of Titus.
Raffaele Stern began a modern restoration of the arch in 1817.
Valadier continued the restoration under Pope Pius VII in 1821, adding new capitals and travertine masonry.
A local ban on Jews walking under the arch was in place until the foundation of the State of Israel in 1947.
In 1997, the ban was rescinded during a Hanukkah event.
The arch has become a symbol of the Jewish diaspora.

design.description: The arch features fluted and unfluted columns, with a large inner archway measuring 8.3 meters in height and 5.36 meters in width.
Spandrels depict personifications of victory; panels show spoils from the Temple in Jerusalem and Titus as triumphator.
19th‑century restorations added new capitals and travertine masonry to distinguish original marble.

art.description: The south inner panel features a detailed menorah, a key symbol of Jewish heritage.
The north inner panel depicts Titus in a chariot, flanked by winged Victory.
